newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African economists see rates down despite gold.
newsitem.headline: S.African economists see rates down despite gold.

text.p: South African economists say they do not expect melting gold prices to influence the central Reserve Bank's monetary policy and most still expect the first of a series of rate cuts between August and October.
"I don't think what is happening on the gold price in any way negates the case for a cut in interest rates over the short term," said Investec Bank group economist Carole Mason.

"There is ample scope for interest rates to start coming down meaningfully in real terms," she said, adding that inflation should fall from an average of around nine percent this year to an average of 6.5 percent in 1998.
Gold was trading at $319.25/319.75 an ounce in early Wednesday trade, after touching a 12-year low of $313.60 bid on July 7.
Though the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's all-gold index fell 23 points to 973 on Tuesday, the rand has remained fairly steady at 4.55 against the dollar.
"If we were to see material rand weakness because of gold, it might negate the case for lower interest rates, but I don't think we are going to see a weaker rand from here," Mason said.
Rand Merchant Bank chief economist Rudolf Gouws said he did not expect the gold price to influence central bank lending rates unless it fell below $300 an ounce.
"If the gold price does plummet, then the Reserve Bank would have to weigh up what a fall in the gold price does to the balance of payments as opposed to the real economy.

"If it was to fall below $300 then it clearly would have implications for the current account of the balance of payments, which would call for higher interests rates. But it would also have an implication for economic growth and jobs, which would call for lower rates," he said.

Industry analysts have said the weak gold price could destroy between 70,000 and 100,000 jobs, although the negative effect could be cushioned by the industry's first productivity-linked wage deal on Monday.

The Chamber of Mines, representing most mine owners, and the National Union of Mineworkers announced agreement on a two-year package linking wage hikes of up to 25 percent to a 20 percent productivity increase.
Gouws said nothing that had happened yet had dented his expectation of an interest rate cut soon.
"What we are going to see over the next few weeks will confirm that the time will be right come August or September.
"I would expect a 100-basis point cut now and I really would not be suprised if, when we get to the year-end, conditions are right for a further cut in the last month or so," he said.

Gouws, in line with the majority of 31 economists polled by Reuters in late June, expects the Reserve Bank's key Bank rate to come down by three percentage points in the current downward cycle by end-1998.
But Mason went further, predicting four one percentage-point cuts before the end of 1998 with the first likely in September.
"Four percent by the end of next year might seem excessive, but the real interest rate is still likely to be quite high by international standards," she said.

Chris Stals, governor of the South Afican Reserve Bank, sought recently to cool speculation about an imminent reduction in the 17 percent Bank rate underpinning the 20.25 prime overdraft rate charged by commercial banks.

"The Reserve Bank will not take the lead to bring interest rates down unless there (is) some slowdown in the rate of increase in the money supply and in bank credit extension," he told Reuters Financial Television last week.

The Bank rate has been steady since November last year. Preliminary May M3 money supply growth was little changed at 15.40 percent while private sector credit growth slowed from 17.4 percent to 16.57 percent in the same period.
Economists continued, however, to predict a cut towards the end of the third quarter with more to follow this year or next.

Nedcor senior economist Magan Mistry said he expected four interest rate cuts before the end of 1998: "We would see two cuts this year and two next year for a 16.25 percent prime rate by the end of next year."
Old Mutual's Gilt Fund portfolio manager Mark le Roux said that despite the gold price slide, he expected the first of three cuts in September or October.
He said interest rates would track inflation, keeping real interest rates constant until South Africa has completed the promised abolition of remaining exchange controls.
